channel.title: Workbench Notes
channel.description: Field notes from a laptop where an AI assistant and local models do the work.

item.title: The laptop is the factory, the edge is the storefront
item.description:
A laptop with a good graphics chip can draft, summarise, tag, translate and render all day for the price of electricity. It is tempting to go one step further and let it serve the results to the world too. That step is where things go wrong.

Three reasons not to serve from home

It sleeps. A lid closes, a battery runs down, an update restarts it. A public site that disappears when someone goes to lunch is not a site.

It usually can't be reached anyway. Many home connections sit behind the provider's shared address, so inbound connections from the internet never arrive, whatever the router is told.

It shares a connection with people. The same line carries video calls and work. An unattended job that fills it is a bad housemate.

The split

So the work divides cleanly:

Stays on the laptop Goes to the edge
Writing, drafting, bulk text work Finished pages
Building the site Serving them, all day, everywhere
Checking it before it leaves Nothing private, ever

The laptop is a factory: noisy, private, switched off at night. The storefront is a pile of finished files on someone else's always-on network. Static files are cheap to host, hard to break and have no server to attack.

When a page needs to do something

Forms and sign-ups need a little code next to the files. The same rule holds. The storefront takes the order and puts it in a queue; the factory collects the queue when it is awake, does the heavy work, and sends back a result. The laptop only ever dials out. Nothing dials in.

The useful consequence is that the expensive part, the thinking, runs on hardware already paid for, and the part that must never go down is the part that costs almost nothing.

item.title: Don't let a model pick its own score
item.description:
A common pattern: hand a model a piece of work and ask for a score out of ten. Work scoring above seven moves on. It looks like judgement. In practice the scores bunch around one comfortable number, and the threshold ends up deciding by noise.

What works better

Ask concrete questions with yes or no answers. Not "how strong is this idea?" but "does the text name who pays?", "is there an existing product that does this?", "does it need a licence to operate?". Small models are far steadier on these.

Compute the score in code. Each answer carries a weight you chose and can read. The model reports facts; arithmetic you can inspect turns them into a decision. When the outcome is wrong you can see which answer was wrong, instead of staring at a 6.5.

Test the judge before trusting it. Keep a set of cases whose right answer you already know, good and bad. Run the judge over them whenever its prompt or model changes. A judge that passes everything is not strict, and a judge that fails everything is not careful. Until you have checked, a pass rate is just a number.

Healthy means useful

The same trap exists one level up. A system that reports "running" every minute can be producing nothing. The health check worth having counts useful output per hour and asks whether each learning loop actually fired.

Where a model's opinion still fits

As a second look that can only add warnings. The gate that decides whether this site may publish works that way: fixed checks decide, and a local model may raise a flag for a reader to look at. It cannot wave anything through.

item.title: A publishing gate an assistant can't talk its way past
item.description:
Publishing is one of the few things an assistant does that can't be taken back. A page can be removed, but a copy may already sit in a cache or an archive. So the rule on this workbench is that going public takes two things, and neither of them is the assistant's own confidence.

One: fixed checks that decide

Every built file is read before it leaves:

  • anything shaped like a credential or key
  • private network addresses, file paths, email addresses
  • a private list of words that must never appear, kept off the public record
  • links that lead nowhere
  • anything loaded from another site

Any hit stops the publish. These are pattern checks, deliberately dull, with test cases for each: a page planted with a fake key must be blocked, and a clean page must pass.

Two: approval for one exact build

Approval attaches to a fingerprint of the built files. Change a comma and the fingerprint changes, and the approval no longer applies. "Approved last week" never covers "edited this morning".

A site can be given standing approval, which suits a notebook like this one. Anything new starts without it.

Then: check the result

After the push, the public address is fetched until it shows the fingerprint that was approved. "It should be live" is not a status. If the check fails, the record says so.

And a way back

Taking a site down is one command. It removes the site and makes its storage private again without deleting anything, so the decision can be reversed in either direction.

None of this is clever. The point is that the steps do not depend on how sure the writer feels.
